row.note: The commentary treats the person himself as the final lost capital; Jesus asks what gain there is in winning the whole world while losing oneself.
The rich man counts years of stored goods as security, but his life is required that night; the scene makes the commentary's hidden loss of principal concrete.
This parallel rich-fool saying has a man plan to fill his stores and lack nothing, then die that night; it sharpens the gap between expected profit and the actual account.
Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing yet does not know it is poor and wretched; this enacts the commentary's loss that can grow unseen beneath apparent success.
After a long interval the master returns and settles accounts with servants entrusted with capital; the parable joins time, work and final reckoning as in the commentary's market image.
The speakers plan to travel, trade and make a profit for a year; James places the commentary's merchant's forecast inside the uncertainty of human life.
James says people do not know tomorrow and their life is a brief vapor; this supplies the finite lifetime that the commentary calls the capital being spent.

row.basis: riches kept to their owner's hurt
row.note: Qohelet says wealth can be kept to the owner's harm, directly matching the commentary's principal that diminishes even while a person appears to possess it.

row.basis: wealth lost in a bad venture
row.note: A failed venture makes the rich man lose his property and leave nothing to his son; this gives the commentary's unprofitable trade a concrete household consequence.

row.basis: wealth amassed without knowing its heir
row.note: The fleeting human heaps up riches without knowing who will gather them; this joins the commentary's passing lifetime to its image of capital that cannot be kept.

row.basis: wages in a bag with holes
row.note: Haggai says people earn wages only to put them into a pierced bag; the image makes the commentary's principal loss visible in an apparently completed day's work.
The rich man says he can now enjoy his goods but does not know how soon he will die and leave them; this is a Jewish parallel to the commentary's false confidence in accumulated capital.
The speaker asks what wealth and pride profited the wicked, then says it passed like a shadow; the text explicitly judges apparent gain by what remains.

row.basis: labor spent on what cannot satisfy
row.note: Isaiah asks why people spend money on what is not bread and labor for what does not satisfy; this directly tests the commentary's unprofitable trade and wasted life-capital.

row.basis: short day, much work, great reward
row.note: Rabbi Tarfon's saying makes the day short, the work much and the reward great; it turns the commentary's time-as-capital image into an explicit account of finite time and labor.

row.basis: an hour of deeds and repentance
row.note: The Mishnah values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world above the whole life of the world to come; it makes each unit of time consequential as in the commentary's account.
The teaching to repent one day before death is answered by the uncertainty of that day, so one should repent today; it gives the commentary's passing time an urgent, practical consequence.
Paul says a person's work may burn and he will suffer loss; this gives the commentary's final accounting a specific test of what a lifetime's work actually yielded.
All things are exposed before God, to whom people must give account; this complements the commentary's contrast between visible success and an unseen loss.
Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory; the wording gives the commentary's comprehensive human deficit a specific moral and theological measure.
God repays each according to deeds; this connects the commentary's person-in-loss to its neighboring ayah's faith and action as the basis of the final account.
Paul says God shows no partiality; with the preceding verse's judgment by deeds, this matches the commentary's refusal to distinguish people by lineage or rank.

row.basis: no preference for rich or prince
row.note: Elihu says God does not favor princes or the rich over the poor, since all are his handiwork; this closely matches the commentary's human class that cuts across social rank.
The merchants shrink the measure, enlarge the shekel and falsify the scales; this is the commentary's specific image of making another person's purchase come up short.

row.basis: buying the needy and selling sweepings
row.note: The merchants exploit the poor and sell the grain's sweepings; this shows the human cost of the under-measure that the commentary describes as taking another's principal.
Proverbs calls a false balance abhorrent and a just weight pleasing to God, joining the commentary's market scale to moral judgment.
Israel is commanded to use just balances, weights and measures; this supplies the positive counterpart to the commentary's trader who secretly gives less than was paid for.

row.basis: Job asks to be weighed fairly
row.note: Job asks to be weighed in just balances so God may know his integrity; the speaker's appeal makes the market scale an image for testing a person's standing.

row.basis: God weighs what people cannot see
row.note: A person's ways seem pure in their own eyes, but the Lord weighs the spirit; this directly answers the commentary's unaware loser who thinks his account is sound.
The solitary worker has no heir, never stops laboring and deprives himself of good; this joins the commentary's isolated human, depleted capital and loss of self.
Qohelet says two are better than one because they have a good return for their toil; this counters the commentary's solitary person in loss with benefit made possible by companionship.
If one falls, the other can lift him; this gives concrete form to the commentary's claim that people leave isolation through mutual relation.

row.basis: speak truth as members of one another
row.note: Paul commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor because they are members of one another; this closely meets the commentary's transition from an isolated human to reciprocal counsel in truth.
The community must exhort one another daily so none is hardened by sin; this links reciprocal counsel to the commentary's time-limited escape from loss.
Paul says what a person sows is what that person will reap; the harvest image makes the commentary's labor-and-account metaphor a concrete rule of consequence.
Sowing to the flesh yields corruption, while sowing to the Spirit yields eternal life; this distinguishes loss from lasting gain by the kind of life invested.
Paul urges persistence in doing good because the harvest comes in due time; this connects the commentary's finite time and good work to patient endurance.
Job calls human life on earth hard service and its days those of a hired worker; this is an unusually close image for the commentary's human spending time as capital and receiving a day's wage.

row.basis: short human life full of trouble
row.note: Job says a human born of woman has few days and much trouble; this gives the commentary's universal human condition a concrete account of brief, burdened life.
Adam must eat from cursed ground through painful toil all the days of his life; this connects the commentary's account of human loss with labor that consumes a finite life.

row.basis: sweat, bread and return to dust
row.note: The human eats bread by sweat until returning to the dust; this places work and death together as the commentary does when it calls time the principal spent.

row.basis: fixed days and an impassable limit
row.note: Job says a person's days are determined and their boundary cannot be crossed; this makes explicit the due term that the commentary associates with each person's final account.
The house built by one who hears and does Jesus' words withstands rain, flood and wind; this brings together the commentary's shelter, storm and distinction by action.
The house of the one who hears but does not do collapses under rain, flood and wind; this is a concrete image of loss tied to the deed that the commentary says changes one's outcome.

Jesus concludes the rich fool story with the person who stores up for himself but is not rich toward God; this states the commentary's distinction between visible accumulation and a sound final account.
The vineyard owner gives the last workers the same denarius as the first; this revises a strict market ledger by making the kingdom's reward rest on the giver's generosity, not hours worked.

Paul contrasts visible things, which are temporary, with unseen things, which are eternal; this illuminates the commentary's tension between the visible human and a loss or value that sight alone misses.

row.basis: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary's source word is ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ; Job calls the wage-bound mortal אֱנוֹשׁ. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while Job's hired-worker image adds the short, allotted human day.

row.basis: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity in loss; Psalm 8 calls the mortal אֱנוֹשׁ and asks why God remembers him, keeping the source's mortality term within a text of divine regard.

The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Daniel's Aramaic humanlike figure appears with the clouds before the Ancient of Days among beastly kingdoms. The table's sound match is unverified; this is a distinct apocalyptic human image, not an identity.

row.basis: Daniel's humanlike figure applied to Jesus
row.note: Jesus applies Daniel's cloud-coming human figure to himself before the council and speaks of vindication and authority; this Christian reading makes the humanlike figure's dominion a reply to defeat and loss.

The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; Qohelet uses מְחַסֵּר for depriving one's own self of good amid fruitless solitary labor. This is a candidate root correspondence, not proof of cognacy.

The source word خُسْرٍ names loss; Daniel says the king was weighed and found חַסִּיר, deficient. The table's unverified Aramaic sound match is reinforced by the passage's exact image of judgment by measure.

The commentary's neighboring exception says وَعَمِلُوا۟, righteous action as labor in the profitable trade; Qohelet asks what gain a person gets from עָמָל beneath the sun, exposing toil without surplus.

The commentary links its neighboring بِٱلْحَقِّ to the day that brings each person to a term; Job uses חֻקָּיו for the fixed bounds of human days. The sound correspondence is unverified, but the allotted-limit motif is specific.

row.basis: אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary says the human named by ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ can fail to see his own loss; Jeremiah calls the heart אָנֻשׁ, desperately sick, and asks who can understand it, joining the table's weak/ill form to self-ignorance.

The source commentary's خُسْرٍ is an account of loss; Proverbs warns that one rushing after wealth will not know that חֶסֶר, want, will come. This joins hidden deficit to pursuit of gain without claiming cognacy.

The source commentary places the human in indefinite loss; Moses describes the promised land as one in which Israel will lack nothing. The table correspondence is unverified, and the verse offers a concrete counter-image of sufficiency.

The commentary's separate source image under عَصْر includes pressing and storm; Job says God can withhold waters until drought or release them until the land is overwhelmed. The table's עָצַר means restrain, a related but unverified sound correspondence.

row.basis: seeing another's eye, missing one's own
row.note: Jesus pictures a person noticing a speck in a brother's eye while ignoring a beam in his own; this echoes the commentary's eye imagery and its warning that the person may not see his own condition.
The hearer who looks in a mirror goes away and forgets what he looks like; this gives a specific image for the commentary's claim that a person may fail to see himself without another's reflection.

row.basis: treasure vulnerable to decay and theft
row.note: Jesus warns that earthly treasure is eaten by moth and rust or stolen; this gives physical form to the commentary's principal that can diminish while a person thinks he is accumulating.

The commentary's separate B008 image records a closed-mouthed vessel under عَصْر; Genesis says God had shut Abimelech's women's wombs, using עָצַר, restrain/close. This is only a shared closure image, not evidence that the Arabic word means loss by closure.

row.basis: finite lifespan, toil and swift passing
row.note: The psalm numbers a human life at seventy or eighty years, marked by toil, then says it passes quickly; this develops the commentary's time-as-principal image into a lifespan.

The commentary's neighboring وَعَمِلُوا۟ names good action; this verse says human years are עָמָל and trouble before they fly away. The table's Arabic ع م ل–Hebrew עמל correspondence is unverified, while the shared labor context is explicit.

row.basis: wealth cannot follow its owner in death
row.note: The rich person takes nothing when he dies and his glory does not descend after him; this matches the commentary's claim that accumulated capital cannot save the person who spent it.

row.basis: nothing carried from birth or toil
row.note: A person leaves as naked as he came and cannot take the fruit of his labor; this supplies a direct account of worldly gain failing at death.
Proverbs warns against wearing oneself out to get rich; this directly questions the commentary's merchant-like pursuit of gain as a use of finite human time.
The wealth a person fixes his eyes on suddenly makes wings and flies away; the image makes visible the commentary's principal that disappears despite apparent accumulation.
One who gains wealth unjustly is likened to a bird hatching what it did not lay and will leave it in midlife; this joins fraudulent gain to the loss of the person who thought it secure.

row.basis: riches fail on the day of wrath
row.note: Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; this contrasts market capital with what can answer at final judgment.
Hannah says the Lord is a God of knowledge and actions are weighed by him; this links the commentary's unseen human account to divine assessment.
The verse says just balances and weights are the Lord's work; this joins the commentary's fair market scale to divine order and judgment.
Micah asks whether wicked treasure remains in a house with a scant measure; the prophet links stored wealth to the short measure that the commentary describes as stealing another's principal.
The Lord asks whether he can acquit someone with wicked scales and deceptive weights; this makes the dishonest trader's reduced measure answerable to judgment.

row.basis: worker longs for shade and wages
row.note: Job compares the sufferer to a slave longing for shade and a hired worker waiting for wages; this continues the commentary's connection between human time, labor and its due.
Job says months of emptiness and nights of misery have been allotted to him; the verse gives a concrete example of living inside loss as an extended condition.

row.basis: a person's allotted day as a hireling's
row.note: Job asks God to turn away until a person's day, like that of a hired worker, is complete; this links the commentary's due term to the end of labor and life.

row.basis: righteous and wicked share one fate
row.note: Qohelet says the same event happens to righteous and wicked alike; this counters the commentary's exception group at the level of earthly outcomes, without directly addressing its afterlife account.

row.basis: fruitful tree that does not wither
row.note: The righteous person is a tree bearing fruit in season whose leaf does not wither; this contrasts the commentary's crop lost to a destructive wind with a life that remains productive.
The wicked are like chaff driven away by wind; this gives a scriptural contrast between the fruitful life and the commentary's image of a life's produce swept away.

row.basis: fruitless tree cut down and burned
row.note: Jesus says a tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this joins the commentary's produce imagery to judgment based on what a life yields.
Jesus says people will give account on judgment day for every careless word; this makes the commentary's comprehensive human reckoning concrete down to speech.

row.basis: dead judged from books by their works
row.note: At the great throne, the dead are judged from opened books according to their works; this is a direct image of the final account that the commentary hears behind loss and deeds.
The verse says humans die once and afterward face judgment; it fits the commentary's image of each person reaching a fixed term and being assessed.

row.basis: postmortem reversal of rich and poor
row.note: Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, and now their conditions are reversed; this shows status and present comfort do not settle the final account.

row.basis: steward reduces a debt by half
row.note: The steward changes an oil debtor's bill from one hundred measures to fifty; unlike the commentary's condemned short measure, the parable places debt reduction inside a crisis strategy for future welcome.

The master praises the dishonest steward's foresight, not his dishonesty; this complicates the commentary's pairing of financial manipulation and loss by distinguishing prudent use of wealth from moral accounting.

row.basis: preserving life leads to losing it
row.note: Jesus says whoever seeks to preserve life will lose it, while whoever loses it will keep it; this gives a distinct saying in which self-protection reverses into the commentary's loss of self.
Paul says the things that were gain to him he counted as loss for Christ; the accounting language directly meets the commentary's distinction between apparent assets and true profit.

row.basis: all things loss for the greater gain
row.note: Paul counts everything as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him; this adds a deliberate revaluation in which relinquishing worldly capital is itself gain.

row.basis: nothing brought in or carried out
row.note: Paul says people bring nothing into the world and can take nothing out; this directly undercuts the assumption that accumulated wealth can secure the self.

row.basis: desire for riches plunges people into ruin
row.note: Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and destructive desires; this connects pursuit of wealth to the commentary's loss of health, faith and self.
James says the rich person's wealth has rotted and garments have been eaten by moths; this gives physical form to the commentary's claim that capital can diminish while held.
Gold and silver rust becomes evidence against their owners and consumes them like fire; the verse links hoarding to a coming reckoning and adds a fire image to the commentary's crop-loss scene.

row.basis: joyful sale for a greater treasure
row.note: The finder sells everything to buy the field with hidden treasure; this reverses the commentary's loss account by showing a total expenditure that is profitable because the acquired good is greater.

row.basis: work of faith and steadfast hope
row.note: Paul remembers the community's work of faith, labor of love and steadfastness of hope; this is a specific Christian formulation of faith joined to action and endurance.
James says faith by itself, without works, is dead; this closely matches the commentary's neighboring exception, where belief is joined to righteous action.
In the vision's contrast between the proud and the upright, the righteous live by faith; this gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's group whose faith keeps them from loss.

row.basis: Paul rereads Habakkuk as gospel principle
row.note: Paul quotes Habakkuk's righteous-by-faith line as the revelation of God's righteousness in the gospel; this Christian reading emphasizes faith as the principle of life alongside the commentary's fuller faith-and-deeds description.
The Didache opens by setting a way of life against a way of death; this gives a concrete early Christian form to the commentary's secondary sense of loss as leaving the right path.

row.basis: self, community and the urgency of now
row.note: Hillel asks who one is if wholly for oneself and, if not now, when; the saying joins the commentary's isolated human, mutual counsel and finite time.

row.basis: do not separate from the community
row.note: The Mishnah warns against separating from the community, trusting oneself until death, or postponing study until free; this connects collective support and urgency to the commentary's path out of isolation and loss.

Akavya ben Mahalalel tells a person to know where he came from and where he goes, and before whom he will give account; this is a direct Jewish formulation of the commentary's human life reaching its reckoning.
Ben Zoma asks who is rich and answers: one who rejoices in his portion; this challenges the commentary's market image by defining wealth through sufficiency rather than accumulation.

row.basis: one deed tips the moral scales
row.note: The Talmud asks each person to see himself as balanced between merit and guilt, so one deed can tip himself and the world; this is a close rabbinic meeting of human action, scales and final consequence.

row.basis: people inscribed by their deeds at the New Year
row.note: The Talmud describes books opened on the New Year and distinguishes the righteous, wicked and intermediate by their inscription for life or death; this gives the commentary's universal verdict and exception group a Jewish judgment-day framework.

The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; the Hebrew speaker says לֹא אֶחְסָר, “I lack nothing,” within the shepherd's provision. The table's sound correspondence is unverified, and the verse supplies a precise counter-image of sufficiency.

row.basis: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Isaiah asks why anyone fears אֱנוֹשׁ, a mortal who dies and is like grass. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while the verse adds human mortality and fear.

row.basis: אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
row.note: The source's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ is linked in the table to Hebrew אנש; Jeremiah calls his wound אָנֻשָׁה, incurable. This is the root's illness/weakness usage, not a claim that the Arabic noun means illness.
